title: The Lighter Brief
overview: A busy Monday: Jensen Huang is back running Nvidia just 11 days after resigning, with Congress lining up questions, and the Army got a court's go-ahead for a controlled blast in Iowa. Closer to home for Charlotte readers, the Thanksgiving Eve parade was called off because of wind, and the city council is weighing a rule requiring air conditioning in rentals. There's also a new breast cancer pill approval and a handy reminder about pet-influencer scams.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia's CEO
stories.summary: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated founder Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, 11 days after he resigned. He stepped down following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman U.S. officials suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. President Trump said he helped persuade the board, and lawmakers from both parties are asking questions about national security.
key_facts: Huang resigned Nov. 12 and was reinstated Monday, Nov. 23.
Nvidia stock rose more than 30% on the news.
Huang is scheduled for closed-door testimony on Capitol Hill on Dec. 1.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer says Democrats will use their 'full power' to investigate.
disputed: Confirmed: Huang resigned after news reports of affairs and has now been reinstated.
Reported but not proven: one relationship was with a Megaspeed executive whom U.S. officials believed had ties to Chinese intelligence.
Nvidia's board says it is 'confident' there is no national security risk. Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and others have publicly questioned what that conclusion is based on.
Trump says he 'convinced' the board. Schumer argues Trump put his own and his allies' financial interests ahead of national security.
stories.why: Nvidia makes many of the chips behind today's AI boom, so who leads it, and how that was decided, matters to the economy and to policymakers in both parties.

stories.headline: Don Toliver's Manchester show evacuated; London date moved to Dec. 15
stories.summary: More than 12,000 fans were safely escorted out of Don Toliver's concert at Manchester's Co-op Live on Sunday night after people reported eye and breathing irritation from an unknown substance. One person went to the hospital for assessment, and police are investigating. Toliver moved his London O2 show to Dec. 15, and Manchester ticket holders are getting automatic refunds.
key_facts: The incident happened shortly after 10 p.m. on Nov. 22.
Medics assessed more than 80 people, according to updated ambulance service figures; one person was taken to the hospital.
O2 London tickets are valid for the new Dec. 15 date.
The Nov. 24 show at OVO Arena Wembley was still listed on the venue's calendar.
disputed: Police initially suspected tear gas but have not confirmed what the substance was.
How the substance got into the arena is still under investigation.
Early reports put the number assessed at about 50; later figures say more than 80.
stories.why: If you had tickets, here's the practical bit: Manchester refunds are automatic and London tickets carry over to Dec. 15.

stories.headline: Rep. Jimmy Gomez to resign after House ethics report
stories.summary: California Democrat Jimmy Gomez says he will resign from Congress on Dec. 1. The bipartisan House Ethics Committee released a report finding substantial evidence that he made unwelcome sexual advances toward a House staffer. Gomez says he strongly disagrees with the findings and the process, but sees no alternative to resigning.
key_facts: Gomez has represented part of Los Angeles since 2017.
He had already lost his reelection race this month to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres.
The Ethics Committee has five Democrats and five Republicans.
The committee said there wasn't enough time to pursue a House sanction before he leaves office.
disputed: Confirmed: the committee's report found substantial evidence of misconduct, and Gomez has announced his resignation.
Gomez disputes the report, saying it left out key parts of his testimony and selectively quoted him.
stories.why: His resignation moves up the change in who represents this Los Angeles district, and the case is part of a wider conversation about workplace conduct on Capitol Hill.

stories.headline: Charlotte's Thanksgiving Eve Parade called off for wind
stories.summary: Organizers canceled the 80th annual Novant Health Thanksgiving Eve Parade in uptown Charlotte. The forecast calls for high winds, strong gusts, rain and cold, which would make the giant balloons, floats and setup equipment unsafe. The parade usually goes on rain or shine, but organizers called this year's conditions exceptional.
key_facts: This would have been the parade's 80th year.
Dozens of parade units had already withdrawn.
Ticket buyers will automatically get a full refund.
stories.why: If you were planning to go, you don't need to do anything to get your money back, and it's a good cue to keep an eye on the holiday forecast.

stories.headline: Army cleared to proceed with controlled Iowa detonation Wednesday
stories.summary: A federal appeals court ruled that the Army can detonate 68 barrels of degraded lead azide, an unstable explosive compound, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Middletown. The court found that the EPA's emergency permit includes adequate safeguards to limit lead dust. Earlier in the day President Trump had paused the plan, but the Army says it is now going ahead Wednesday morning with support from state officials.
key_facts: The blast covers about five tonnes of material that officials say could explode on its own.
Safeguards include barriers, weather restrictions, advance public notice and air monitoring.
The date has changed several times since the original plan for last Friday.
Gov. Kim Reynolds supports going forward. Gov.-elect Rob Sand says the decision belongs to the administration and is asking for more public information.
stories.why: People who live or work nearby have been advised to avoid the area and stay indoors during the detonation, and environmental groups and the incoming governor are pushing for more transparency.

stories.headline: Two former Jamaican PMs offer to help cool tensions in Parliament
stories.summary: Former prime ministers P.J. Patterson and Bruce Golding say they would be willing, if asked, to mediate disputes in Jamaica's House. The disagreements are between government and opposition lawmakers, and between the Opposition and House Speaker Juliet Holness. Initial talks have already started.
key_facts: The disputes led to one MP being suspended.
A censure motion against the Speaker has been tabled for debate.
The Opposition alleges bias in the Speaker's rulings.
stories.why: It's a nice moment when former leaders from opposite sides offer to help lower the temperature.

stories.headline: Jamaica's government says no hurricane relief funds are missing
stories.summary: Responding to an Auditor General's report on Jamaica's disaster agency, ODPEM, Local Government Minister Desmond McKenzie said no money donated for Hurricane Melissa relief is missing. He acknowledged problems at the agency, including some food supply issues he said cannot be defended. Opposition Leader Mark Golding has called for accountability and for ODPEM's director general to resign.
key_facts: The governing JLP says its ODPEM reforms predate the audit and points to a review published in January.
The police commissioner says all donated Starlink devices are accounted for.
The opposition PNP wants Commander Alvin Gayle to step down.
stories.why: How relief money and supplies are handled affects how quickly communities recover after storms.

stories.headline: Charlotte weighs requiring AC in homes
stories.summary: Charlotte City Council is considering a housing code change that would require homes to have cooling that can keep at least two rooms at 80 degrees or below from May through September. A majority of council members seemed supportive, but several raised concerns about costs for homeowners on fixed incomes. A vote could come soon.
key_facts: Repairs would be required within 48 hours, and violations would be treated as imminently dangerous.
The rule would apply to both existing homes and new buildings.
Supporters say a window unit would count; central air isn't required.
The city has already given out about 200 window units in emergency situations.
stories.why: If it passes, renters would gain a clear right to a cool room in summer, and landlords and homeowners would have new responsibilities.
